At ModernWallet, we show the math in the guides we publish here, starting with a $10,000 loss. If your losses exceed your gains, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) lets you deduct up to $3,000 of the excess from other income each year ($1,500 if married filing separately). You carry the rest forward. The saving equals the tax rate on the gains the loss cancels, so a loss against gains taxed at 0% saves nothing. Most of the benefit is a deferral, because the replacement investment starts with a lower cost basis. Buying the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale triggers the wash sale rule and blocks the deduction. Tools for this journey Stock Capital Gains Tax Calculator → What Tax Loss Harvesting Can Deduct Each Year Tax loss harvesting works by selling an asset for less than its adjusted basis and claiming the difference as a capital loss. IRS Topic 409 says an asset's basis is generally its cost, and a sale for more than that basis is a capital gain. Losses from selling personal-use property, such as a home or car, are not tax deductible. A capital loss on an investment cancels capital gains. If losses are still left over, you can claim the lesser of $3,000 ($1,500 if married filing separately) or your total net loss from line 16 of Schedule D against your other income. Any net loss above that limit carries forward to later years. The holding period sets the type of loss. IRS Topic 409 treats an asset held more than one year as long-term and one held one year or less as short-term. The type matters because the two are taxed differently. Net short-term capital gains are taxed as ordinary income at graduated rates. Most net capital gain is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%. IRS Topic 409 names higher maximum rates for a few gains: 28% for collectibles and section 1202 stock, and 25% for unrecaptured section 1250 gain. What a Harvested Loss Is Worth at 0%, 15% and 20% A harvested loss is worth the tax rate on the gain it cancels, multiplied by the size of the loss. In our internal modeling, we ran a $10,000 harvested loss against $10,000 of long-term gains taxed at 0%, 15% and 20%. The saving came out to the rate times the loss, which is nothing at 0%. Long-term gains rate Gain cancelled Federal tax saved 0% $10,000 $0 15% $10,000 $1,500 20% $10,000 $2,000 The inputs are a $10,000 loss, $10,000 of long-term gain and one federal rate per row. The model leaves out ordinary-income rates, state tax, the net investment income tax and transaction costs, so every figure is illustrative. Your rate depends on your 2026 taxable income, and that test includes the gain itself. IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32 sets these 2026 ceilings for the 0% and 15% rates: Married filing jointly: 0% up to $98,900, 15% up to $613,700 Head of household: 0% up to $66,200, 15% up to $579,600 Married filing separately: 0% up to $49,450, 15% up to $306,850 All other individuals: 0% up to $49,450, 15% up to $545,500 Above the 15% ceiling for your filing status, the 20% rate applies. A year with losses and no gains works differently. With a $10,000 net capital loss and no gains, our model deducts $3,000 against other income and carries $7,000 forward. A married person filing separately deducts $1,500. The cash value of that deduction depends on the rate on your other income, which we did not model. A tax professional can apply your rate. Tax Loss Harvesting Usually Defers Tax to a Later Year Tax loss harvesting usually moves tax to a later year, because the replacement you buy has a lower basis than the investment you sold. In our internal modeling, a share bought for $10,000 and sold at $7,000 produces a $3,000 loss. A replacement bought for $7,000 has a $7,000 basis. Sell that replacement later for $10,000 and you realize a $3,000 gain. The gain equals the loss you harvested. The tax comes back unless the rates differ between the two years or the gain is never realized. A later rate above today's rate makes the deferral cost more than it saved. Some cases, such as a 0% year, a basis step-up at death or a gift to charity, can change the result. A tax professional can explain how they apply to your return. The Wash Sale Rule and Tax Loss Harvesting in an IRA The wash sale rule blocks a harvested loss when, within 30 days before or after the sale, you acquire substantially identical stock or securities. IRS Publication 550 lists four ways to trigger it: Buy substantially identical stock or securities Acquire substantially identical stock or securities in a fully taxable trade Acquire a contract or option to buy substantially identical stock or securities Acquire substantially identical stock for your individual retirement arrangement (IRA) or Roth IRA A purchase of substantially identical stock by your spouse or by a corporation you control also creates a wash sale. In a taxable account, the disallowed loss is added to the cost of the new shares, which becomes their basis. The added cost postpones the deduction until you sell the new shares, and the holding period of the shares you sold carries over to them. Publication 550 gives this example. You buy 100 shares of X stock for $1,000 and sell them for $750. Within 30 days you buy 100 shares for $800. You cannot deduct the $250 loss, and your new basis is $1,050. When the repurchase is for an IRA or Roth IRA, Publication 550 does not add the disallowed loss to the cost of the new stock. A tax professional can explain what that means for your loss. No mechanical formula defines substantially identical, as our wash sale rule guide explains. You weigh all the facts and circumstances, and stock of two different corporations is ordinarily not substantially identical. When Tax Loss Harvesting Does Not Pay Tax loss harvesting saves nothing now when the gains it cancels would have been taxed at 0%. Four cases reduce or remove the benefit: Your 2026 taxable income, including the gain, is at or below the 0% ceiling for your filing status, so the loss cancels gain that carried no federal tax. You have no gains, so the loss lowers other income by at most $3,000 a year ($1,500 if married filing separately) and the rest waits in carryover. You buy back the same or a substantially identical security inside the 30-day windows, including in an IRA. Your tax rate when you sell the replacement is higher than the rate on the gains you cancelled. The rules above describe sales in taxable accounts that you report on Form 8949. Losses inside an IRA or another tax-deferred account are a question for a tax professional. If you need a decision on your own holdings, a tax professional can apply these rules to your return. Our answer would change if your bracket differs from the ones modeled, or if the $3,000 limit or the wash sale rule changes. The IRS pages cited above do not cover state tax treatment, the net investment income tax or cryptocurrency, so a tax professional can add those to your figures. Our wash sale rule guide covers how brokers report wash sales across accounts. Our tax tips guide covers other year-end moves. How to Report a Harvested Loss You report a harvested loss on Form 8949, Sales and Other Dispositions of Capital Assets, which IRS Topic 409 names as the form for most sales of capital assets. Each sale's gain or loss is figured there and then totalled on Schedule D. IRS Publication 550 has you combine your net short-term gain or loss from Schedule D line 7 with your net long-term gain or loss from line 15. The total goes on Part III, line 16. A net loss allowed against other income goes on line 7a of Form 1040, Form 1040-SR or Form 1040-NR. Any loss above the yearly limit is tracked with the Capital Loss Carryover Worksheet. That worksheet appears in Publication 550 and in the IRS Instructions for Schedule D , with separate lines for short-term and long-term carryovers. To figure the tax on one specific sale before you report it, use our Stock Capital Gains Tax Calculator . Our Takeaway For a US taxpayer with realized capital gains taxed at 15% or 20%, harvesting a loss saves 15 or 20 cents of federal tax per dollar of loss now. With gains taxed at 0% it saves nothing, and with no gains it saves tax only on the first $3,000 of loss a year. That conclusion applies to taxable accounts and rests on IRS rules plus our worked arithmetic. The answer changes if you buy the same or a substantially identical security within the 30-day windows, including in an IRA. It also changes if a higher future rate makes the deferral cost more than it saved. List your 2026 realized gains and losses, and check your trade history for any repurchase inside the 30-day windows before you harvest a loss. If your case is not simple, take that list to a tax professional before any tax loss harvesting sale. Frequently asked questions Is it possible to sell stocks at a loss to reduce taxes? Yes. Selling stock below its adjusted basis creates a capital loss that cancels capital gains. IRS Topic 409 lets you deduct up to $3,000 of any excess against other income ($1,500 if married filing separately). The deduction is blocked if you buy substantially identical stock within 30 days before or after the sale. Do I get $3,000 back from a stock loss? No. The $3,000 limit is a deduction that lowers your taxable income on line 7a of Form 1040. The cash you save depends on the tax rate on that income, and any loss above the limit carries forward to later years. Is there a downside to tax loss harvesting? Yes, the saving is usually a deferral. The replacement investment has a lower basis, so in our $10,000 example the $3,000 harvested loss returns as a $3,000 gain when the replacement is sold at $10,000. A wash sale repurchase postpones the deduction, and a higher future tax rate can make the deferral cost more than it saved. Does tax loss harvesting reduce taxable income? Yes, up to a limit. After your losses cancel your capital gains, the remaining loss lowers your taxable income on line 7a of Form 1040. The limit is the lesser of $3,000 ($1,500 if married filing separately) or your total net loss. The rest carries forward to later years. Is tax loss harvesting just deferring taxes? Mostly, yes. Because the replacement starts at a lower basis, the gain you avoid now comes back when you sell it, unless the tax rates differ or the gain is never realized. A tax professional can explain how a 0% year, a basis step-up at death or a gift to charity apply to you. Can short-term losses offset long-term gains? Yes, Schedule D combines them into one net result. IRS Publication 550 has you combine net short-term gain or loss from line 7 with net long-term gain or loss from line 15 into one total on line 16. Any carryover keeps its short-term or long-term character, and the Schedule D instructions show a separate carryover line for each. You get a deduction or employer exclusion on money going in, tax-free earnings while the money sits in the account, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified medical expenses. At ModernWallet, we show the math in every guide we publish, so we list the exact 2026 dollar limits from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the rules that end each break. For 2026, an eligible person with a qualifying high-deductible health plan (HDHP) can contribute up to $4,400 for self-only coverage or $8,750 for family coverage, plus $1,000 at age 55 or older. Contributions stop with the first month of Medicare enrollment. A withdrawal for anything other than qualified medical expenses is taxed as income and, before age 65, can carry an additional 20% tax. Tools for this journey Retirement calculators → HSA Triple Tax Advantage Limits for 2026 The HSA triple tax advantage is three separate tax breaks that apply when money goes in, while it earns and when it comes out for medical bills. IRS Publication 969 describes each break. The 2026 dollar limits come from IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-19 (Rev. Proc. 2025-19) . Contributions: Publication 969 says you can deduct contributions that you, or anyone other than your employer, make to your HSA, even if you do not itemize deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040). Contributions from your employer, including those made through a cafeteria plan, may be excluded from your gross income instead. Earnings: Interest and other earnings on the assets in the account are tax free. Withdrawals: Distributions are tax free when you use them to pay qualified medical expenses. You report contributions on Form 8889 with your Form 1040. The HSA trustee reports contributions on Form 5498-SA and distributions on Form 1099-SA. Employer contributions appear on your Form W-2 in box 12 with code W. The 2026 figures below apply only when your coverage meets the IRS definition of an HDHP. 2026 figure Self-only coverage Family coverage HSA contribution limit $4,400 $8,750 Added amount at age 55 or older $1,000 (total $5,400) $1,000 for each eligible individual age 55 or older (no family total shown) HDHP minimum annual deductible $1,700 $3,400 HDHP maximum deductible plus out-of-pocket costs (premiums not counted) $8,500 $17,000 Arithmetic on those two IRS figures: an eligible self-only person age 55 or older can contribute $4,400 + $1,000 = $5,400 in 2026. We do not total the family limit with the $1,000 here, because IRS Publication 969 has spouse-specific rules. The out-of-pocket cap counts deductibles, co-payments and other amounts. Premiums do not count. If your plan uses a provider network, Publication 969 says only in-network deductibles and out-of-pocket expenses count toward the limit. The contribution limit covers all your HSAs combined. If you have more than one HSA, your total contributions to all of them cannot exceed the limit. You must also reduce what you can contribute by any employer contributions that are excluded from your income. Who Can Contribute to an HSA Only an eligible individual covered by a qualifying HDHP can contribute to an HSA, and for 2026 the plan must meet the deductible and out-of-pocket figures in the table above. A self-only plan with a deductible under $1,700 does not meet the 2026 definition. Neither does a family plan whose deductible and out-of-pocket costs can run past $17,000. Medicare enrollment ends new contributions. Publication 969 says that beginning with the first month you are enrolled in Medicare, your contribution limit is zero. Excess contributions carry a 6% excise tax, covered in the next section. The Medicare rule can apply to earlier months. If you delay applying for Medicare and your enrollment is backdated, contributions made during the retroactive period count as excess contributions. If you are near Medicare enrollment, our Medicare Savings Programs guide explains that your state can pay your Medicare premiums through a Medicare Savings Program if you qualify. The last-month rule lets some people contribute a full year's amount. Under Publication 969, if you have family HDHP coverage on the first day of the last month of your tax year, you can contribute the full-year limit. The last-month rule carries a testing period that begins with the last month of your tax year and ends on the last day of the 12th month after that month. If you fail to stay an eligible individual during the testing period, for any reason other than death or disability, you owe tax on the extra amount. You include in income the contributions you could only make because of the last-month rule. You also owe a 10% additional tax, figured in Form 8889, Part III. Where the Three Tax Breaks End Four IRS rules limit the three tax breaks. Excess contributions: Publication 969 says you generally pay a 6% excise tax on excess contributions. The tax applies to each tax year the excess stays in the account, and you report it on Form 5329. Non-medical withdrawals: You can take a distribution at any time, but only amounts used exclusively for qualified medical expenses are tax free. Other distributions are subject to income tax and may be subject to an additional 20% tax. Insurance premiums: You may not use HSA funds to pay for insurance, with four exceptions. The exceptions are long-term care insurance, health care continuation coverage, health care coverage while you receive unemployment compensation, and Medicare and other health care coverage if you are 65 or older. Premiums for a Medicare supplemental policy such as Medigap do not qualify. Double counting: You cannot deduct, as an itemized deduction on Schedule A, qualified medical expenses equal to the tax-free distribution from your HSA. The 20% additional tax does not apply to distributions made after you become disabled, reach age 65 or die. Income tax on a non-medical withdrawal still applies after 65. Only the extra 20% goes away. Year-to-Year Carryover and Portability HSA funds do not expire. Publication 969 says amounts left at the end of the year generally carry over to the next year, and you do not have to make withdrawals each year. The contributions stay in the account until you use them, and the HSA itself is generally exempt from tax. The account is portable. It stays with you if you change employers or leave the work force. You can roll over amounts from Archer medical savings accounts (MSAs) and from other HSAs into an HSA. Rollovers are not subject to the annual contribution limit, and you do not need to be an eligible individual to roll over from an existing HSA to a new HSA. HSA Triple Tax Advantage Compared with an FSA or Roth IRA Two other ModernWallet guides compare the HSA triple tax advantage with a flexible spending account (FSA) and with a Roth individual retirement account (IRA). Our HSA vs. FSA comparison puts the two health accounts side by side. Our HSA vs. Roth IRA comparison does the same for the HSA and the Roth IRA. What the HSA Triple Tax Advantage Does Not Cover IRS Publication 969 and Rev. Proc. 2025-19 do not cover these questions: State income tax treatment of HSAs. Your own tax saving, which depends on your marginal tax rate and your state. A tax professional can apply your state's rules and your marginal rate to your return. The 2026 figures above do not fit three readers. No qualifying HDHP: Without a qualifying HDHP, the contribution limits above do not apply to you. The HSA vs. FSA comparison covers the FSA side. Already enrolled in Medicare and wanting to contribute: Your contribution limit is zero from the first month of enrollment. You do not need to be an eligible individual to roll over from an existing HSA to a new HSA. Expecting to spend the money on non-medical costs before 65: Those withdrawals owe income tax and may owe the additional 20% tax. The HSA vs. Roth IRA comparison covers the retirement-account side. Our answer would change if the IRS publishes new contribution limits or changes the HDHP deductible and out-of-pocket rules. Every dollar figure here is for 2026 only. For other planning moves at tax time, our tax tips guide lists more. Our Takeaway An HSA fits an eligible person on a qualifying HDHP who expects to use the money for qualified medical expenses. The deduction, the tax-free earnings and the tax-free medical withdrawals all apply to the same dollars. That answer rests on IRS Publication 969 and Rev. Proc. 2025-19. The answer changes in three cases. Your plan may not be a qualifying HDHP. Your state may tax HSAs differently, and a tax professional can apply your state's rules. You may also expect to need the money for non-medical costs before 65, when a withdrawal costs income tax plus a possible 20% additional tax. Contributions end once Medicare enrollment starts. Confirm your plan meets the 2026 high-deductible definition in Rev. Proc. 2025-19 before you count on the HSA triple tax advantage, then compare the HSA with an FSA or a Roth IRA . Frequently asked questions What does a triple tax advantage mean? It means one account gets three tax breaks. For an HSA, IRS Publication 969 says contributions are deductible, or excluded from income when your employer makes them. Earnings are tax free, and withdrawals are tax free when you use them for qualified medical expenses. Do HSA funds expire? No. Amounts left at the end of the year generally carry over to the next year, and you do not have to make withdrawals each year. The HSA also stays with you if you change employers or leave the work force. What are the advantages of an HSA? The advantages are the three tax breaks, plus carryover and portability. Rollovers from another HSA do not count against the annual contribution limit. What is one potential downside of an HSA? A withdrawal for anything other than qualified medical expenses is taxed as income and may carry an additional 20% tax before age 65. You also need a qualifying HDHP to contribute. Your contribution limit drops to zero from the first month of Medicare enrollment. Are HSA contributions tax deductible if I do not itemize? Yes. Publication 969 says you can deduct contributions you or someone other than your employer make even if you do not itemize deductions on Schedule A. Employer contributions, including those made through a cafeteria plan, may be excluded from your gross income instead, and you report contributions on Form 8889. Is an HSA worth it? An HSA can be worth it if you are eligible, covered by a qualifying HDHP and expect to spend the money on qualified medical expenses. Unspent amounts carry over to the next year. New contributions are not allowed once Medicare enrollment starts. A non-medical withdrawal before 65 costs income tax plus a possible 20% additional tax. A tax professional can apply your state's rules and your marginal rate. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. mainEntity.name: What does a triple tax advantage mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: It means one account gets three tax breaks. For an HSA, IRS Publication 969 says contributions are deductible, or excluded from income when your employer makes them. Earnings are tax free, and withdrawals are tax free when you use them for qualified medical expenses.

mainEntity.name: Do HSA funds expire?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Amounts left at the end of the year generally carry over to the next year, and you do not have to make withdrawals each year. The HSA also stays with you if you change employers or leave the work force.

mainEntity.name: What are the advantages of an HSA?

acceptedAnswer.text: The advantages are the three tax breaks, plus carryover and portability. Rollovers from another HSA do not count against the annual contribution limit.

mainEntity.name: What is one potential downside of an HSA?

acceptedAnswer.text: A withdrawal for anything other than qualified medical expenses is taxed as income and may carry an additional 20% tax before age 65. You also need a qualifying HDHP to contribute. Your contribution limit drops to zero from the first month of Medicare enrollment.

mainEntity.name: Are HSA contributions tax deductible if I do not itemize?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Publication 969 says you can deduct contributions you or someone other than your employer make even if you do not itemize deductions on Schedule A. Employer contributions, including those made through a cafeteria plan, may be excluded from your gross income instead, and you report contributions on Form 8889.

mainEntity.name: Is an HSA worth it?

acceptedAnswer.text: An HSA can be worth it if you are eligible, covered by a qualifying HDHP and expect to spend the money on qualified medical expenses. Unspent amounts carry over to the next year. New contributions are not allowed once Medicare enrollment starts. A non-medical withdrawal before 65 costs income tax plus a possible 20% additional tax. A tax professional can apply your state's rules and your marginal rate.

At ModernWallet, we show the math behind each money decision. BRRRR is investor shorthand for buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat. The new loan can be as large as the post-repair appraisal times the lender's loan-to-value (LTV) limit, and the cost of that loan comes out of it. In our internal modeling, a rental with $193,000 invested (purchase price, closing costs and repairs) needed an appraisal of about $262,585 to return all of it. That assumes a 75% LTV and a 2% refinance cost. The strategy stops working when the appraisal comes in low, when a lender rule limits the loan, or when the new loan payment is more than the rent. Tools for this journey Real estate calculators → How the BRRRR Method Works Step by Step The BRRRR method runs in five steps, and your cash comes back at the fourth step, the refinance. Investors describe the strategy with this shorthand: Buy a property that needs work. Rehab it with repairs. Rent it. Refinance it with a new loan based on the repaired value. Repeat with the cash the refinance returns. Build the refinance math before you buy. Two numbers decide the deal. The first is the total cash you put in: purchase price, closing costs and repairs. The second is the cash the new loan hands back: the appraised value times the lender's LTV limit, minus the cost of the new loan. If the second number is smaller, the gap stays tied up in the property. The refinance in step 4 is a cash-out refinance. Under the Fannie Mae Selling Guide , a cash-out refinance can take equity out of the property for any purpose. The new loan must either pay off the existing mortgage with a new first mortgage on the same property, or be a new mortgage on a property with no mortgage lien. A house bought with cash and carrying no lien fits that second case. Fannie Mae sets the maximum LTV for a cash-out refinance in its Eligibility Matrix. The 75% figure in our example below is an assumption of ours, so swap in the limit your lender quotes. The BRRRR Method in a Worked Example In our internal modeling, we ran one hypothetical $150,000 purchase with $40,000 of repairs through a refinance at three appraised values, and getting all $193,000 back took an appraisal of about $262,585. That result assumes a 75% LTV and a 2% cost on the new loan. Both are our assumptions, and neither is a lender limit or a Fannie Mae figure. These are the inputs we used: Purchase price: $150,000, paid in cash Purchase closing costs: $3,000 Repairs: $40,000 Total cash invested: $193,000 Assumed LTV on the appraised value: 75% Assumed cost of the new loan: 2% of the loan amount The table shows two refinance paths. The standard path assumes a loan of 75% of the appraised value. The capped path applies our reading of Fannie Mae's delayed financing limit. Fannie Mae does not address repair spending, so ask the lender how it counts repair costs. Appraised value Standard loan (assumed 75% LTV) Net after 2% cost Cash left in deal (standard) Capped loan (delayed financing reading) Cash left in deal (capped) $200,000 $150,000 $147,000 $46,000 $150,000 $46,000 $230,000 $172,500 $169,050 $23,950 about $156,122 $40,000 $260,000 $195,000 $191,100 $1,900 about $156,122 $40,000 The break-even works backward from the cash invested. Dividing $193,000 by 0.98 (one minus the 2% cost) gives a loan of about $196,939, and dividing that loan by 0.75 gives an appraisal of about $262,585. That appraisal is 1.36 times the $193,000 you put in. On the standard path, each extra $10,000 of appraised value adds $7,350 of net proceeds ($10,000 × 0.75 × 0.98). The $230,000 appraisal falls about $32,585 short of break-even, so $23,950 stays in the deal. We did not buy or refinance a property, and every dollar amount in this example is illustrative. Lender Seasoning Rules That Slow the BRRRR Refinance Fannie Mae requires at least one borrower to be on title for six months before a cash-out refinance disburses, and it adds two more timing and listing rules. These rules come from Selling Guide section B2-1.3-03, dated December 10, 2025: Title: at least one borrower must have been on title for at least six months before the disbursement date of the new loan. Fannie Mae lists exceptions under "Ownership of the Property." Existing first mortgage: a first mortgage paid off by the refinance must be at least 12 months old, measured from its note date to the new loan's note date. The rule does not apply to subordinate liens or to buying out a co-owner under a legal agreement. Listing: a property that was listed for sale must come off the market on or before the disbursement date of the new loan. If you financed the purchase with a first mortgage on the house, the refinance cannot pay that loan off until it is 12 months old. A cash purchase leaves no first mortgage to pay off. In that case the six-month title rule and the delayed financing exception set the timing. Fannie Mae's rules apply to loans sold to or guaranteed by Fannie Mae. Portfolio loans and other loan types follow each lender's own rules, which are not covered here. If you are weighing a cash-out refinance against a home equity line of credit (HELOC), our cash-out refinance vs. HELOC comparison sets the two side by side. The Delayed Financing Exception Inside Six Months Fannie Mae's delayed financing exception lets a borrower who bought the property within the past six months take a cash-out refinance, with the new loan capped at the documented purchase investment. The six months run from the purchase date to the disbursement date of the new loan. Every one of these requirements must be met: The original purchase was an arms-length transaction. You meet Fannie Mae's borrower eligibility requirements. A settlement statement shows no mortgage financing was used for the purchase. A title search shows no existing liens. The sources of the purchase funds are documented. If the purchase money came from an unsecured loan or a loan on another asset, such as a HELOC on another property, all cash-out proceeds must pay off or pay down that loan. The refinance settlement statement must show it. Gift funds used for the purchase cannot be reimbursed with the new loan. The loan can be no more than the documented initial investment in purchasing the property plus financed closing costs, prepaid fees and points on the new loan. It also cannot exceed the maximum LTV on the current appraised value. Our reading of that wording is that repair spending falls outside the "initial investment in purchasing the property." Fannie Mae's guide does not address repair spending either way, so this interpretation is ours. A lender could read the rule differently. In our internal modeling, we capped the loan at the $153,000 purchase investment ($150,000 price plus $3,000 closing costs) plus 2% financing of the new loan's costs. That cap comes to about $156,122. At the $230,000 and $260,000 appraisals, net proceeds were $153,000 and the $40,000 of repair money stayed in the deal. At the $200,000 appraisal, the 75% limit produced a smaller loan than the cap. The loan was $150,000 and $46,000 stayed in. Ask the lender how it counts repair costs under this exception before you buy, and read the exception's full text in Fannie Mae's Selling Guide . Depreciation on a Repaired BRRRR Rental Residential rental buildings are generally depreciated over 27.5 years under the general depreciation system (GDS), according to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) in Publication 527. The alternative depreciation system (ADS) uses 30 years. Both periods cover the building and its structural components. Land is not part of the depreciation basis. For a BRRRR property, the depreciation start date follows the repairs. In another Publication 527 example, a house bought and extensively repaired was ready for rent on July 5, advertised in July and rented starting September 1. The IRS treats that house as placed in service in July, when it was ready and available for rent, so depreciation can begin then. Our scenario does not split the $150,000 price into land and building, so it produces no depreciation figure. See our rental property tax deductions guide . When the BRRRR Method Stops Working The BRRRR method stops returning your cash when the appraisal comes in low, when a lender cap limits the loan, or when the new payment is more than the rent brings in. The $200,000 row in our model shows a low appraisal. The loan is $150,000, net proceeds are $147,000 and $46,000 stays in the deal. Any appraisal below about $262,585 leaves some cash behind at our assumed 75% LTV. A lender cap can hold back cash even when the appraisal is high. On our reading of the delayed financing exception, a refinance inside six months returns about the purchase money. It leaves the $40,000 of repairs in the deal at both the $230,000 and $260,000 appraisals. Ask the lender how it counts repair costs. The new loan payment can also outrun the rent. Our model leaves out rent, the new interest rate, the monthly payment, property taxes, insurance, vacancy and holding costs, so it says nothing about cash flow. Price the new payment, taxes and insurance against the rent before you plan the refinance. The BRRRR method does not fit these readers: Someone who cannot wait out six months on title, or 12 months when the refinance pays off a first mortgage on the house. Someone whose plan depends on an appraisal that has not happened yet. Someone who needs the repair money back inside six months. If you want to own real estate without a rehab or a refinance, our comparison of a real estate investment trust (REIT) vs. a rental property lays out that route. Three inputs would change our answer: the lender's actual LTV limit, the appraisal on the repaired house, and any change to Fannie Mae's seasoning or delayed financing rules. A lender LTV limit above our 75% assumption lowers the appraisal needed to break even. A limit below 75% raises it. Our Takeaway The BRRRR method can return most or all of your cash only when the post-repair appraisal is high enough for the loan to cover the money in the deal. In our modeled example, that took an appraisal of about $262,585 on $193,000 invested, at our assumed 75% LTV and 2% refinance cost. The rules come from Fannie Mae's Selling Guide and IRS Publication 527, and the math comes from our own scenario. The strategy fits an investor who can wait out lender seasoning and buys below the finished value. It does not fit anyone whose plan depends on an appraisal the house may not reach, or on a payment the rent cannot cover. It also does not fit anyone who needs a refinance inside six months to recover repair spending, based on our reading of the delayed financing wording. Ask the lender how it counts repair costs. The lender's real LTV limit and the appraisal can move this verdict either way. Ask a lender for its seasoning rule and maximum investment-property LTV, then rerun the BRRRR method math with your own purchase, repair and appraisal numbers before you buy. Frequently asked questions How much money do you need to start the BRRRR method? There is no verified standard amount, because the cash you need equals the purchase price, repairs and closing costs you carry until the refinance. In our modeled example, that was $193,000: a $150,000 cash purchase, $3,000 of closing costs and $40,000 of repairs. How much comes back depends on the appraisal and the lender's LTV limit. Is it BRRR or BRRRR? Investors use both spellings. BRRRR stands for buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat. BRRR describes the same strategy without the final "repeat" step. What is the 2% rule for rental property? The 2% rule is an unverified investor rule of thumb that none of our listed sources defines, so we do not treat any figure from it as a standard. Run the break-even math from the worked example above with your own purchase, repair and appraisal numbers. What is the 70% rule for BRRRR? The 70% rule is another unverified investor rule of thumb that none of our listed sources defines, and we do not endorse a figure from it. The number that decides a BRRRR deal is the appraisal needed for the new loan to cover your cash. Divide your total cash invested by one minus the loan cost, then by the lender's LTV limit, as shown in the worked example. Is BRRRR better than flipping? BRRRR fits a goal of keeping a rental, and flipping fits a goal of selling. A flip ends with a sale of the property. A BRRRR ends with a refinance loan and a rental you keep, so you also take on the new loan payment. How long does the BRRRR method take? Fannie Mae's floor is six months on title before a cash-out refinance disburses, and 12 months if the refinance pays off an existing first mortgage. Inside six months, Fannie Mae's delayed financing exception allows a cash-out refinance if all its requirements are met, and it caps the loan at your documented purchase investment plus financed loan costs. Repair time and the time to find a tenant are not published in the sources here, so we do not estimate them. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. You'll learn how retirement accounts, HSAs, and tax-loss harvesting can lower your bill, as well as how tax brackets and the standard deduction shape every decision. This guide provides general information, not tax advice. Rules change, and your situation may need review by a CPA or enrolled agent. Once you've put these moves in place, see TurboTax vs. TaxAct to find out which filing software actually applies them correctly at the lowest cost. Tools for this journey 401(k) growth → Roth IRA → High-yield savings → Tip 1: Fund tax-advantaged accounts first The biggest tax break most people miss is simply funding tax-advantaged accounts up to the annual limit. For 2026, the IRS lets you contribute up to $24,500 to a 401(k), plus an $8,000 catch-up at age 50 or older. Traditional 401(k) contributions lower your taxable income today. IRAs offer a smaller but useful boost. The 2026 IRA contribution limit is $7,500, with a $1,100 catch-up at age 50 or older. Use our 401k calculator and Roth IRA calculator to see how each choice grows over time. Always contribute enough to your 401(k) to capture the full employer match first, because that is a 100% return that you cannot get anywhere else. Tip 2: Use an HSA for the triple tax break A Health Savings Account (HSA) is the only account that offers a triple tax advantage . IRS Publication 969 confirms all three: contributions are tax-deductible, growth is tax-free, and qualified medical withdrawals are tax-free. You need a high-deductible health plan to qualify. For 2026, the IRS lets you contribute up to $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for family coverage. Many people miss the biggest opportunity by spending the HSA balance right away instead of investing it. If you can pay medical bills from other cash, let the HSA grow, then withdraw for those past expenses years later, tax-free. Tip 3: Consider tax-loss harvesting each fall Tax-loss harvesting means selling investments at a loss to offset gains and reduce your tax bill. The IRS lets you use realized losses to cancel out realized capital gains dollar for dollar. Any extra loss can offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income each year, and any remainder carries forward to future years. Watch the wash-sale rule. If you buy the same or a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss is disallowed. Review your taxable brokerage account each November, not just in December, so you have time to act without rushing. Tip 4: Watch your bracket transitions The federal income tax uses marginal brackets, which means only the income above each threshold is taxed at that bracket's rate. This is not the same as your average tax rate. Understanding the difference helps you plan year-end income and deductions. A small change can matter near a bracket edge. Timing a Roth conversion, a bonus, or a large deduction can keep you in a lower bracket. If you are near a threshold, delaying $5,000 of income or accelerating a deduction can save real money. Our high-yield savings calculator helps you plan year-end cash moves. Tip 5: Standard versus itemized deduction Most filers now take the standard deduction because it is larger than their itemized total. You should itemize only when your qualifying deductions exceed the standard amount. Common itemized items include state and local taxes (capped at $10,000), mortgage interest, and charitable gifts. One planning move: bunching. If your itemized total is close to the standard, group two years of charitable gifts into one year to clear the threshold, then take the standard next year. A donor-advised fund can hold the gift now and distribute it over time — see how it compares to a private foundation if you're giving at a larger scale, or read how a donor-advised fund works . Check the current standard deduction on IRS.gov before you plan. The 2026 Standard Deduction for Married Couples Filing Jointly A married couple filing jointly gets a $32,200 standard deduction for 2026, exactly double the $16,100 amount for a single filer, compared to $24,150 for head of household. Filing jointly clears more income before any tax applies, which is one reason most married couples file jointly rather than as married filing separately, where each spouse is capped at the lower $16,100 amount. A couple where one or both spouses are 65 or older adds $1,650 per qualifying spouse on top of the $32,200 base, so two spouses both 65 or older reach a combined $35,500 standard deduction before a single itemized deduction enters the picture. That extra amount doubles again to $3,300 per spouse if a spouse is also legally blind. Run the bunching strategy above against your own itemized total using the higher $32,200 (or $35,500) baseline before deciding it's worth the extra recordkeeping. Already behind on taxes? Here are your options → The tips above are proactive planning — they work if you're current on filing and payments. If you already owe back taxes, the IRS has statutory relief programs the public rarely hears about: Offer in Compromise settles the debt for less than owed, an installment agreement spreads it over 72+ months and cuts the failure-to-pay penalty in half, Currently Not Collectible suspends collection during hardship, First Time Abate wipes penalties, and the 10-year Collection Statute Expiration Date under IRC §6502(a)(1) writes off what isn't collected in time. Our tax resolution calculator maps your specific situation to the right program, and the back taxes impact calculator shows the mortgage, passport, and credit consequences of leaving it unaddressed. Frequently asked questions What is the best tax tip most people miss? The best tax tip most people miss is funding tax-advantaged accounts up to the annual IRS limit. A 401(k) contribution can lower your taxable income today, and an HSA offers a triple tax break. Capturing the full employer match on a 401(k) is the highest-return money move you can make. How much can I contribute to a 401(k) in 2026? The 2026 401(k) contribution limit is $24,500, per the IRS. If you are 50 or older, you can add an $8,000 catch-up contribution for $32,500 total. Ages 60 to 63 have a special $11,250 catch-up under SECURE 2.0. What is tax-loss harvesting? Tax-loss harvesting is selling losing investments to offset realized capital gains. The IRS lets you cancel gains dollar for dollar and use up to $3,000 of extra loss against ordinary income each year. Any remaining loss carries forward to future tax years. How does an HSA give a triple tax advantage? An HSA gives three tax breaks per IRS Publication 969: deductible contributions, tax-free growth, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified medical expenses. You need a high-deductible health plan to contribute. The 2026 contribution limits are $4,400 for self-only and $8,750 for family coverage. Should I take the standard or itemized deduction? You should take whichever is larger. Most filers now take the standard deduction because it exceeds their itemized total. Itemize when your state and local taxes (capped at $10,000), mortgage interest, and charitable gifts add up to more than the standard. What is the standard deduction for married filing jointly in 2026? $32,200 for 2026, double the $16,100 single-filer amount. A couple where one or both spouses are 65 or older adds $1,650 per qualifying spouse on top, reaching $35,500 if both spouses qualify. Is this tax advice? mainEntity.name: What is the best tax tip most people miss?

acceptedAnswer.text: The best tax tip most people miss is funding tax-advantaged accounts up to the annual IRS limit. A 401(k) contribution can lower your taxable income today, and an HSA offers a triple tax break. Capturing the full employer match on a 401(k) is the highest-return money move you can make.

mainEntity.name: How much can I contribute to a 401(k) in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 2026 401(k) contribution limit is $24,500, per the IRS. If you are 50 or older, you can add an $8,000 catch-up contribution for $32,500 total. Ages 60 to 63 have a special $11,250 catch-up under SECURE 2.0.

mainEntity.name: What is tax-loss harvesting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tax-loss harvesting is selling losing investments to offset realized capital gains. The IRS lets you cancel gains dollar for dollar and use up to $3,000 of extra loss against ordinary income each year. Any remaining loss carries forward to future tax years.

mainEntity.name: How does an HSA give a triple tax advantage?

acceptedAnswer.text: An HSA gives three tax breaks per IRS Publication 969: deductible contributions, tax-free growth, and tax-free withdrawals for qualified medical expenses. You need a high-deductible health plan to contribute. The 2026 contribution limits are $4,400 for self-only and $8,750 for family coverage.

mainEntity.name: Should I take the standard or itemized deduction?

acceptedAnswer.text: You should take whichever is larger. Most filers now take the standard deduction because it exceeds their itemized total. Itemize when your state and local taxes (capped at $10,000), mortgage interest, and charitable gifts add up to more than the standard.

mainEntity.name: What is the standard deduction for married filing jointly in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: $32,200 for 2026, double the $16,100 single-filer amount. A couple where one or both spouses are 65 or older adds $1,650 per qualifying spouse on top, reaching $35,500 if both spouses qualify.

mainEntity.name: Is this tax advice?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, this guide is general information for education, not tax advice. Tax rules change and vary by state, filing status, and income. Talk to a CPA, enrolled agent, or other qualified tax professional before making major moves like Roth conversions or large charitable gifts.

acceptedAnswer.text: Math errors, missing income like 1099s, and missing the filing deadline are among the most common tax mistakes. See our 9 common tax mistakes guide for the full list and how to avoid each one.

mainEntity.name: How much is the Child Tax Credit worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Up to $2,200 per qualifying child for 2026, with as much as $1,700 refundable even if you owe no federal tax. See our Child Tax Credit guide for the income phase-out and how to claim it.

That creates a window spanning 61 calendar days in total, so it is neither strictly a 30-day nor a 60-day rule in practice. In a taxable account, the disallowed loss is added to the cost basis of your replacement shares, so the deduction waits until you sell those shares. At ModernWallet, we find that what readers get wrong most often is assuming the rule only looks forward in time. Buying replacement shares two weeks before you sell a losing lot disallows the loss just as buying them two weeks after does. Trading bots and AI agents make this easy to miss, because they can buy the stock back in a separate account without asking you. Tools for this journey Investment calculators → The Mechanics of the 30-Day Window Before and After Under Internal Revenue Code Section 1091 , the statutory window begins 30 days before the date of the sale at a loss and ends 30 days after that date. Counting the day of the sale itself alongside the 30 days preceding it and the 30 days following it yields an arithmetic total of 61 days. If you execute a sale on July 15 at a capital loss, any acquisition of substantially identical assets between June 15 and August 14 can trigger the restriction. The rule covers more transactions than direct purchases of common stock. IRS Publication 550 establishes that entering into a contract or option to acquire substantially identical stock or securities counts as an acquisition for wash sale purposes. This includes purchasing call options or warrants on the stock you just sold at a loss. Selling bonus-award shares at a loss while receiving another award of substantially identical stock within 30 days also disallows the deduction. The rule also reaches beyond transactions registered exclusively in your personal name. If you sell stock at a loss and your spouse buys substantially identical shares within the window, the IRS treats the transaction as a wash sale. The same restriction applies if a corporation you control purchases the replacement shares. The rule also applies under Section 1091(e) to losses on closing a short sale if you sell substantially identical stock or enter another short sale within 30 days before or after closing the position. Basis Adjustments and Holding-Period Additions When a wash sale occurs, the disallowed loss is not permanently eliminated from your taxable holdings. Publication 550 instructs you to add the disallowed dollar amount directly to the cost basis of the newly acquired replacement shares. This upward basis adjustment postpones your tax deduction until you ultimately dispose of those replacement shares in a future, unwashed transaction. Publication 550's Example 1 shows the math. Suppose you purchase 100 shares of stock X for $1,000. You later sell those 100 shares for $750, realizing a $250 loss. Within 30 days of that sale, you purchase 100 replacement shares of stock X for $800. Because the purchase falls inside the wash sale window, your $250 loss is not deductible on your current tax return. Instead, you add the $250 disallowed loss to the $800 purchase price, giving your new 100 shares an adjusted cost basis of $1,050. Along with the basis increase, the holding period of your original stock attaches to your replacement stock. If you held the initial shares for ten months before selling at a loss, your newly acquired shares automatically inherit that ten-month period on day one. This provision helps determine whether a subsequent sale qualifies for long-term treatment as outlined in our ordinary income vs. capital gains tax comparison . The Facts and Circumstances of Substantially Identical Securities The tax code does not provide a mechanical, mathematical formula for what makes two financial instruments substantially identical. Publication 550 states that you must evaluate all facts and circumstances in each situation. Ordinarily, stocks or securities issued by one corporation are not considered substantially identical to those issued by an entirely separate corporation. Exceptions exist when corporate structures merge or overlap. For example, securities issued by predecessor and successor corporations involved in a corporate reorganization can be treated as substantially identical under IRS scrutiny. Bonds or preferred stock are not ordinarily substantially identical to the same company's common stock. Convertible bonds or convertible preferred stock can be, depending on their relative values, price changes and other circumstances. For mutual funds and exchange-traded funds, Publication 550 does not publish a bright-line test. Publication 550 does not say whether two funds that track the same index, such as two S&P 500 funds from different managers, are substantially identical. Because no safe-harbor list exists for fund pairs, a replacement fund that tracks a different market segment carries less doubt; our portfolio rebalancing guide covers choosing one. Partial Share Matching and the IRA Trap When the quantity of shares bought within the window does not match the quantity sold, Publication 550 requires a lot-by-lot matching sequence. You must match the replacement shares bought with an equal number of shares sold, starting with the earliest purchases made during the window. A wash sale on a partial position disallows only the loss attributable to the matched replacement lots. Publication 550 demonstrates this with an exact dated scenario. An investor buys 100 shares of company M on September 20, 2024, for $5,000. On December 13, 2024, the investor buys 50 shares for $2,750, and on December 20, 2024, buys 25 shares for $1,125. On January 3, 2025, the investor sells the original 100 shares for $4,000, creating an overall $1,000 loss. Because 75 shares were acquired within the preceding 30 days, the loss on 75 shares ($750) is disallowed, while the loss on the remaining 25 shares ($250) is immediately deductible. The basis of the December 13 lot increases to $3,250 ($2,750 plus $500), and the basis of the December 20 lot increases to $1,375 ($1,125 plus $250). The rule is harsher if you buy the replacement shares in an IRA or a Roth IRA. Revenue Ruling 2008-5 , published in Internal Revenue Bulletin 2008-3, covers this case. If you sell stock at a loss and have your IRA or Roth IRA buy substantially identical stock within 30 days before or after the sale, the loss is disallowed under Section 1091. The individual's basis in the IRA is not increased. Because that basis does not go up, you never recover the disallowed loss. Cross-Account Trading and Autonomous Bot Execution Brokerage firms are only required to calculate and report wash sales for covered securities sharing the same CUSIP number within a single brokerage account. Under the official Form 1099-B instructions , a broker is permitted, but not required, to aggregate transactions across different accounts. If you sell a stock at a loss at one brokerage and buy it back two weeks later at another, your Form 1099-B may show no disallowed loss. Publication 550 says you still cannot deduct it. The same gap applies when software buys for you. As explained in our breakdown of Robinhood agentic trading , an AI agent can trade in its own account. If that agent buys a stock you sold at a loss in your main account within 30 days, you have a wash sale that your Form 1099-B may not flag. An agent trading in the Robinhood 24 Hour Market can make that purchase overnight, before you check your account. Robo-advisors that harvest tax losses raise the same question, and our best robo-advisors roundup covers how each handles tax-loss harvesting. You remain personally responsible for identifying and adjusting every matching trade on your return regardless of automated origin. Tax Reporting on Form 1099-B and Form 8949 When a wash sale happens within a single taxable brokerage account involving identical CUSIPs, your financial institution will detail the adjustment directly on Form 1099-B. Box 1g will show the exact dollar amount of the wash sale loss disallowed. To report these transactions accurately to the IRS, you transfer the figures to Form 8949, Sales and Other Dispositions of Capital Assets, using either Part I for short-term trades or Part II for long-term holdings. Per the Form 8949 instructions , you list the details of the transaction, enter the capital "W" in column (f) to designate a wash sale, and write the disallowed loss as a positive number in column (g). Entering the positive number in column (g) reduces the net capital loss claimed on that trade line. If the number in box 1g of Form 1099-B is incorrect because the repurchase happened in another account, or if a wash sale occurred that the broker did not track, you must input the correct calculation in column (g). If your actual wash sale disallowance is lower than what the broker stated, the IRS instructions require you to attach an explanatory statement to your tax return explaining why the broker figure was adjusted. Our tax tips guide covers the records to keep before you file. Digital Asset Treatment and Pending Legislation The text of Section 1091 specifies that wash sale limitations apply to sales or trades of "stock or securities." Under current federal tax guidance, the IRS classifies digital assets as property , citing Notice 2014-21. Because general property transactions follow general tax principles rather than the specific provisions of Section 1091, conventional cryptocurrencies have historically not been restricted by statutory wash sale disallowance rules. However, tokenized securities represent a distinct category subject to standard reporting. Under the official Form 1099-DA instructions , brokers must report disallowed wash sale losses in box 1i for transactions involving tokenized securities treated as stock or securities under Section 1091. Same-account and same-CUSIP reporting principles apply to these digital securities exactly as they do to traditional equity assets. Pending federal legislation could extend the rule to most digital assets. On September 16, 2026, the House Ways and Means Committee voted 38 to 5 to approve H.R. 10357, known as the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act, according to an Unchained report on H.R. 10357 . If enacted, the bill would extend wash sale rules to traded digital assets other than qualified dollar stablecoins, retroactive to sales occurring after September 14, 2026. A Forvis Mazars analysis notes that broader House and Senate action remains uncertain, leaving the bill as unpassed legislation rather than settled law. Mark-to-Market Elections for Qualifying Active Traders Day traders are subject to the wash sale rule unless they make a mark-to-market election. IRS Topic 429 says traders without that election remain subject to both the capital loss limits and the wash sale rules. If you trade the same stock in and out many times, disallowed losses keep rolling into your newest shares, so your return can show taxable gains in a year your account balance fell. To bypass these restrictions, a qualifying trader must make a formal mark-to-market election under Section 475(f) of the tax code. IRS Topic 429 confirms that traders who make a valid Section 475(f) election are not subject to wash sale rules or regular capital loss deduction limits. Trader tax status is a separate question from the pattern day trader rule , which is a margin rule at your broker. Publication 550 also notes that dealers in stock or securities are exempt from wash sale disallowance for losses incurred in the ordinary course of business. Talk to a tax professional before you make a Section 475(f) election. Practical Execution Tactics to Avoid Unintended Disallowance The simplest way to stay clear is to wait until the 31st day after the sale to buy back; for a July 15 sale, that is August 15. Also make no purchase of the same stock in the 30 days before the sale. If you want to stay invested in the meantime, you can buy a different holding, such as a broad fund. Publication 550 gives no test for funds, so the facts-and-circumstances standard decides whether a replacement is substantially identical. Automatic purchases count as purchases. If a recurring buy purchases more shares of the stock within 30 days of your loss sale, the matching rule disallows the loss on that many shares, so pause recurring buys of that stock around the sale. If you run a trading bot or an AI agent, tell it not to buy any ticker you plan to sell at a loss, from 30 days before the sale until the 31st day after it. Once that window passes, check your trade log before you let it trade the ticker again. Frequently asked questions Is the wash sale rule 30 or 60 days? The statutory rule covers 30 days before and 30 days after your sale date, spanning an arithmetic total of 61 calendar days when including the sale day itself. Because replacement purchases made in the 30 days leading up to the sale trigger disallowance just like purchases made afterward, the rule operates over this combined two-sided window. Can I sell a stock and buy it back within 30 days? Yes, you can legally buy it back at any time, but doing so within 30 days disallows your ability to claim the capital loss on your tax return. Instead, your disallowed loss is added to the cost basis of the newly purchased shares, deferring the tax deduction until those new shares are sold in an unwashed transaction. Can I claim a loss after a wash sale? You cannot claim the loss in the tax year the wash sale occurs, but the loss is usually deferred rather than lost forever. Because the disallowed amount gets added to the replacement stock's cost basis, you will realize the tax benefit when you eventually sell the replacement position, provided that final sale is not another wash sale. How do day traders avoid wash sales? Day traders avoid wash sales by either waiting 31 calendar days before re-entering a losing position, trading completely different instruments, or qualifying for Trader Tax Status and making a Section 475(f) mark-to-market election. A valid mark-to-market election exempts qualifying traders from wash sale rules entirely under IRS Topic 429. Does the wash sale rule apply to crypto? Current tax law treats digital assets as property rather than stock or securities, so standard cryptocurrency transactions are not subject to Section 1091 wash sale rules today. However, tokenized securities are covered, and H.R. 10357, a bill approved by a House committee, would apply the rule to most digital assets sold after September 14, 2026, if enacted. Does the wash sale rule apply across different brokerage accounts? Yes. The wash sale rule applies across all your accounts, including IRAs, and to purchases by your spouse or a corporation you control. While individual brokers only report wash sales that occur within the same account for the exact same CUSIP, you are legally responsible for tracking and reporting cross-account wash sales on Form 8949. Health Savings Account (HSA) vs Flexible Spending Account (FSA): Side-by-Side Health Savings Account (HSA) Flexible Spending Account (FSA) 2025 contribution limit $4,300 individual / $8,550 family $3,300 (healthcare FSA) Account ownership You own it — portable when you leave your employer Employer-owned — typically forfeited when you leave Rollover / carryover Full balance rolls over every year, indefinitely "Use it or lose it" — up to $660 carryover OR 2.5-month grace period (employer's choice) Eligible health plan required Yes — must be enrolled in an HDHP No — available with most health plan types Investment option Yes — invest in stocks, ETFs, and mutual funds above the cash threshold No — cash-only, no investment component Tax advantage Triple: pre-tax contributions + tax-free growth + tax-free withdrawals Double: pre-tax contributions + tax-free qualified withdrawals (no growth) Funds available day 1 Only what you've contributed so far this year Full annual election amount available on day 1 of coverage 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? Choose an HSA if your employer offers a high-deductible health plan — the triple tax advantage, unlimited rollover, and long-term investment potential make it one of the most powerful savings vehicles in the tax code. Choose an FSA if your health plan doesn't qualify for an HSA, you need the full year's funds available immediately in January, or you have predictable annual medical expenses you know you'll spend. If your employer offers a Limited-Purpose FSA (dental and vision only), you can pair it with an HSA to get benefits from both — but a standard healthcare FSA and an HSA cannot be held simultaneously. How an HSA works A Health Savings Account (HSA) is a personal tax-advantaged account you own permanently. Contributions go in pre-tax, grow tax-free when invested, and come out tax-free when used for qualified medical expenses — the only triple tax advantage in the U.S. tax code. The key eligibility requirement: you must be enrolled in a High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP). In 2025, an HDHP is defined as a plan with a minimum deductible of $1,650 for self-only coverage or $3,300 for family coverage. If your employer doesn't offer an HDHP option, you can't open an HSA. The rollover rule is the HSA's most underrated feature. Unlike an FSA, your full balance carries forward every year without limit. A 35-year-old who contributes $4,300/year for 30 years and invests at a historical 8% average return would accumulate over $525,000 — and all of it is tax-free for qualified medical expenses. Use the investment calculator to model HSA growth at your contribution level. At age 65, the HSA transforms into something resembling a Traditional IRA: you can withdraw for any purpose and pay ordinary income tax on non-medical withdrawals, with no additional penalty. Medicare premiums are always qualified HSA expenses, tax-free. How an FSA works A Flexible Spending Account (FSA) is an employer-sponsored benefit that lets you set aside pre-tax dollars for qualified medical, dental, and vision expenses without requiring a specific type of health plan. The key practical feature: your full annual election amount is available from day one — even before you've contributed those payroll deductions. The trade-off is the "use it or lose it" rule. Unspent FSA balances at year-end revert to your employer. The IRS allows employers to offer one of two relief options — a carryover of up to $660 to the following plan year, or a 2.5-month grace period — but not both, and not every employer offers either. The FSA is entirely employer-controlled. If you leave your job mid-year, your remaining FSA balance is generally forfeited unless you elect COBRA continuation coverage. This portability gap is the sharpest practical difference between the two accounts. For families with known large annual medical expenses — scheduled surgeries, braces, or a new baby's pediatric costs — the FSA's front-loading can actually be an advantage. You can charge $3,300 in January and repay it through payroll the rest of the year, effectively getting an interest-free loan from your employer. The HSA as a long-term retirement savings tool The most underused HSA strategy is treating it as a "stealth IRA" for healthcare costs in retirement. The approach: max the HSA each year, invest the balance in a low-cost stock index fund, pay current medical expenses out of pocket, and save every receipt. At retirement, you use those saved receipts to reimburse yourself from the HSA — tax-free, with no time limit on reimbursements for old expenses. Medicare premiums, long-term care insurance, and most healthcare costs in retirement are qualified HSA expenses and can be paid tax-free. The compounding advantage is substantial. An HSA invested in an S&P 500 index fund from age 35 to 65 outperforms the same dollars in a taxable savings account by roughly 30–40% on an after-tax basis, solely from eliminating capital gains and dividend taxes along the way. A non-obvious implication: the HSA is the only savings account where you can contribute pre-tax, earn returns tax-free, AND withdraw tax-free — making its effective return higher than a Roth IRA for qualified medical expenses. See the net worth calculator to factor healthcare costs into your long-term financial picture. When an FSA beats an HSA The FSA wins in several scenarios that most comparison articles overlook. First: predictable large early-year expenses. If you're scheduling a $3,000 surgery in January, the FSA lets you access the full $3,300 immediately and repay through payroll deductions — the HSA would only have what you'd contributed since January 1. Second: when your employer's health plan doesn't qualify for an HSA. Many popular employer plans — PPOs with low deductibles, HMOs — don't meet the HDHP threshold. If your only option is a $1,000-deductible plan, HSA is off the table and FSA is the only pre-tax health savings option available. Third: predictable annual spend with no desire to invest. If you reliably spend exactly your FSA election on annual healthcare costs, the FSA's simplicity (no investment decisions, no investment threshold to manage) is genuinely adequate. The triple tax advantage only matters if you have a long-enough time horizon for tax-free growth to accumulate. For most people under 50 with an HDHP option, the HSA still wins on math. But the FSA wins on practicality when health plan constraints or near-term cash flow are the primary concern. Use the retirement calculator to factor both accounts into your long-term savings plan. Frequently asked questions Can I have both an HSA and an FSA at the same time? Not a standard healthcare FSA and an HSA simultaneously — IRS rules prohibit it. However, you can pair an HSA with a Limited-Purpose FSA (LPFSA), which covers only dental and vision expenses. You can also hold a Dependent Care FSA (for childcare costs) alongside an HSA — that's a different type of FSA entirely and has no conflict with HSA eligibility. What happens to my HSA if I switch from an HDHP to a regular health plan? Your existing HSA balance stays yours permanently. You just can't make new contributions while enrolled in a non-HDHP plan. The funds already in the account can still be used tax-free for qualified medical expenses at any age, with no deadline. If you switch back to an HDHP later, you can resume contributions. What happens to my FSA if I leave my job? Your FSA balance is generally forfeited when you leave your employer unless you elect COBRA continuation coverage to maintain FSA access through year-end. The FSA is employer-owned — unlike an HSA, you can't take it with you. This is one of the strongest arguments for spending your FSA down before leaving a job and for contributing conservatively if job security is uncertain. Is an HSA or FSA better for taxes? The HSA is better for taxes in almost every scenario where you qualify. It provides a triple tax advantage: pre-tax contributions reduce your taxable income, growth is tax-free when invested, and withdrawals for medical expenses are tax-free. An FSA gives you the first and third benefit but not tax-free growth (no investment option). For someone in the 22% tax bracket saving $4,300/year in an HSA, the immediate income tax savings alone is about $946 — plus investment growth over time. What qualifies as a medical expense for HSA and FSA? Both accounts cover the same IRS-defined list: doctor visits, prescription drugs, dental care, vision care (including LASIK), mental health services, surgery, hospital fees, and many medical devices. After the 2020 CARES Act, over-the-counter medications and menstrual care products are eligible for both without a prescription. Cosmetic procedures, gym memberships, and non-prescription vitamins are generally not qualified expenses. The full list is in IRS Publication 502. By Jonathan Velez , Personal Finance Writer & Editor · Reviewed against primary sources · Updated June 25, 2026 The core difference between a cash-out refinance and a HELOC is what happens to your first mortgage. A cash-out refinance replaces your existing mortgage with a new, larger loan, then pays you the difference in cash. Investors who buy a rental, repair it and refinance to pull their cash back out use this structure in the BRRRR method . A HELOC keeps your first mortgage intact and adds a second, revolving line of credit on top of it. Choose a cash-out refinance when today's rates are near or below your current rate. Choose a HELOC when your existing rate is low and you want to protect it. Cash-Out Refinance vs HELOC: Side-by-Side Cash-Out Refinance HELOC Loan structure New, larger first mortgage that replaces your old one Second loan that sits behind your first mortgage Rate type Usually a fixed rate on the whole new balance Usually a variable rate tied to the prime rate Effect on existing mortgage Repays and replaces it at today's rate Leaves it fully intact, rate untouched How you get the money One lump sum at closing Revolving credit line you draw as needed Closing costs About 2% to 5% of the new loan amount Low or sometimes zero upfront costs Rate behavior Locked for the life of the new loan Can rise or fall with the prime rate Best when Your current rate is high, or you want one fixed payment Your current rate is low and you want flexible access 📣 Building in finance? Put your product in front of readers comparing options on this page. Advertise With Us → Which should you choose? Pick a cash-out refinance if your current mortgage rate is at or above today's rates and you want one fixed payment. Pick a HELOC if your existing rate is low, since a refinance would reprice your entire balance at a higher rate. A homeowner holding a very low mortgage rate almost always keeps it and uses a HELOC for extra cash. Both loans use your home as collateral, so missing payments can lead to foreclosure. How Each Option Works A cash-out refinance and a HELOC both turn home equity into cash, but through opposite structures. A cash-out refinance pays off your current mortgage with a new, bigger loan. You get the difference in cash at closing. You now have one payment at one new rate for the entire balance. A HELOC is a second loan that leaves your first mortgage alone. It works like a credit card secured by your home. You draw money during a set period and pay interest only on what you use. Both options usually cap your combined loan-to-value at about 80% to 85%. That limits how much equity you can tap. To see how much you may qualify for, try our mortgage calculator , or see our HELOC calculator guide for the exact borrowing-limit math and what your payment looks like once the draw period ends. The Rate Trap: Why Cash-Out Refinance Can Cost More The biggest hidden risk in cash-out refinance vs HELOC is repricing your whole loan. A cash-out refinance replaces your entire mortgage at today's rate. Suppose you owe $250,000 at 3%. You want $50,000 in cash. A cash-out refinance turns your full $300,000 balance into a loan at today's higher rate. You just repriced money you already had cheaply. A HELOC avoids this. Your $250,000 stays at 3%. Only the new $50,000 carries the higher HELOC rate. This is the key decision rule. When your current rate is much lower than today's rates, a HELOC almost always wins on total interest. Run both scenarios in our budget planner before you decide. Costs, Rates, and Payments Compared Closing costs and rate type separate these two options as much as structure does. A cash-out refinance carries closing costs of about 2% to 5% of the new loan. On a $300,000 loan, that is $6,000 to $15,000. In return, you usually lock a fixed rate and one predictable payment. A HELOC often has low or zero upfront costs. But its rate is variable and tied to the prime rate. Your payment can rise if the prime rate climbs, and a HELOC rate is often higher than a first-mortgage rate. So you trade certainty for flexibility. Weigh both against your long-term plan in our net worth tracker . Is the Interest Tax Deductible? Interest on either loan is deductible only if you use the money to improve your home. This rule comes from the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act and IRS Publication 936. You can deduct the interest if you use the cash to buy, build, or substantially improve the home that secures the loan. A kitchen remodel or an addition can qualify. You cannot deduct the interest if you use the money to pay off credit cards, buy a car, or cover tuition. The purpose of the funds decides the deduction, not the loan type. This rule applies equally to a cash-out refinance and a HELOC. Always confirm your situation with a tax professional, since limits and records matter. Which Should You Choose? Your existing mortgage rate is the deciding factor in cash-out refinance vs HELOC. It usually matters more than closing costs or convenience. Choose a cash-out refinance when today's rates are at or below your current rate. You may lower your rate and pull cash in one move. It also suits people who want a single fixed payment. Choose a HELOC when your current rate is low and you want to protect it. It also fits ongoing needs, like a renovation you fund in stages. If you are still weighing a refinance itself, compare 15-year vs 30-year mortgage and fixed vs ARM mortgage terms first. Frequently asked questions Is a HELOC or cash-out refinance better if I have a low mortgage rate? A HELOC is almost always better if your mortgage rate is low. A cash-out refinance replaces your entire balance at today's higher rate. A HELOC keeps your low first-mortgage rate and charges the higher rate only on the new money you borrow. Does a cash-out refinance replace my current mortgage? Yes. A cash-out refinance pays off your existing mortgage and replaces it with a new, larger loan. You receive the difference in cash at closing and make one payment at the new rate on the full balance. How much can I borrow with each option? Both usually cap your combined loan-to-value at about 80% to 85% of your home's value. On a $400,000 home, that leaves roughly $320,000 to $340,000 in total loans, minus what you already owe on your mortgage. Is the interest on a cash-out refinance or HELOC tax deductible? The interest is deductible only if you use the money to buy, build, or substantially improve the home that secures the loan, per IRS Publication 936. Using the funds for other purposes, like debt payoff, makes the interest nondeductible. Which has lower closing costs, a HELOC or a cash-out refinance? A HELOC usually has lower closing costs, often little to nothing upfront. A cash-out refinance typically costs 2% to 5% of the new loan amount. But a HELOC carries a variable rate that can rise over time. Can I lose my home with either option? Yes. Both a cash-out refinance and a HELOC use your home as collateral. If you miss payments, the lender can foreclose. Borrow only what your budget can safely repay, even if rates rise on a HELOC.
